newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seen seeking changes in Finnish Kesko/Tuko deal.
newsitem.headline: EU seen seeking changes in Finnish Kesko/Tuko deal.

text.p: The European Commission will only clear the acquisition by Finnish wholesaler and retailer Kesko Oy of domestic rival Tuko Oy if changes are made to the deal, a European Union source said on Wednesday.
"Yes, of course it will be changed," the source said in response to a question on whether it would need to be modified to win Commission clearance.
The Commission, which vets mergers and other corporate deals to see whether they may harm competition in the 15-nation bloc, fears the deal will lead to a dominant market position.
"The remedies must correct that," the EU source added, without giving details on what changes the Commission was likely to seek.
The deadline for a Commission decision whether to approve the acquisition is in late November.
In Helsinki, Kesko chief executive officer Eero Kinnunen said he did not expect the EU executive to block the deal, which was announced in May. But he expected it to ask for changes.
"Obviously there will be some changes. I have a feeling that these will concern the relation between us and the shopkeepers," Kinnunen told Reuters.
He said there were "no hints whatsoever" that the Commission may ban the deal, something which it has done only five times since the EU merger regulation came into force in 1990.
Kesko and Tuko are active in Finland in the wholesale and retail of daily consumer goods as well as of specialty goods.

Kinnunen said the Commission feared that the group could get a dominant position on the market as it regards Kesko as a chain store. However, Kesko sees itself as a wholesaler and a supplier to independent shopkeepers.

"Kesko has a totally different view and Kesko will give a statement of defence and negotiate with the Commission on changes to the merger arrangement so that it could approve it," Kesko said in a statement.

The Commission signalled that it was worried about the deal when it opened an in-depth, second phase investigation in July following the initial one-month routine review, saying it could lead to high market shares in Finland.
Most mergers are cleared after the first month and the fact that the Commission starts a detailed investigation usually means that it must be changed.
"Why do we enter a second stage? It is because we have problems and we want remedies," the source said, adding that the Commission had also received comments from competitors.

The deal only came under the jurisdiction of the Commission after the Finnish Office of Free Competition decided to ask it in June to investigate the case as Finland does not have its own merger regulation.
